name: Revisionist Zionism
summary: Revisionist Zionism, founded by Ze'ev Jabotinsky in the 1920s, demanded an openly stated Jewish state with a Jewish majority on both banks of the Jordan, to be secured by military strength behind an iron wall of force. It rejected socialism and class struggle in favour of national unity, private enterprise and compulsory arbitration, and was institutionally embodied in Betar, the Irgun, Herut and later Likud. Its mainstream favoured liberal parliamentary government and civil rights for Arabs as a minority, while an Irgun wing was harder-line.
scope: Jabotinsky's Revisionist movement (Hatzohar, the New Zionist Organization, Betar) and its Herut and Likud heirs under Begin, based on the Iron Wall essay, the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry and the 1977 Likud platform. Excludes Lehi's fascist-leaning wing and later religious-settler Zionism. Economic and social questions the movement did not address are answered as neutral or low confidence.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Herut later backed national health insurance, but the Revisionist founding program was built around private initiative, so adherents are split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Later Herut supported a minimum wage while the Jabotinsky-era program stressed private capital and national over class interests; no settled line.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Revisionists favoured private initiative and private capital with minimal state involvement, against Labor's Histadrut economy.

public-ownership.rationale: Revisionism opposed the Labor movement's collectively owned economic sector and favoured private enterprise in industry.

unions-good.rationale: Revisionists rejected class struggle, built a rival labor body to the Histadrut and sought compulsory arbitration with strikes banned during state-building.

property-fundamental.rationale: Jabotinsky held private property necessary for liberty, though national goals could override it in practice.

cut-welfare.rationale: Herut later accepted social legislation while the early program was pro-capital; adherents are split and the sources are thin.

worker-ownership.rationale: Collective worker ownership was the Labor Zionist model that Revisionists opposed in favour of private enterprise and class cooperation.

strong-leader.rationale: Jabotinsky's centralised, leader-led movement drew comparison with European right-wing movements, and he doubted democracy outside England.

state-harmful.rationale: The movement's whole purpose was to build a Jewish state, which Jabotinsky said was the main thing.

empower-police-military.rationale: Military strength was central: the iron wall doctrine and the Jewish Legion and army demands.

more-religion-public.rationale: Revisionism was neutral on religious questions, with Jabotinsky saying only that a state mattered, not whether it was Orthodox.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The New Zionist Organization aimed at reviving the Jewish state and language, and Betar taught glorification of the nation and its way of life.

gradual-change.rationale: Revisionism was a revision of gradual practical Zionism, demanding an explicit state goal and mass immigration at once.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Jabotinsky relied on force and British power rather than international consent, and Likud rejected outside-imposed solutions and UN Resolution 242.

nation-first.rationale: The movement put national interests above class and foreign pressure, with Likud pledging no handover of Judea and Samaria.

open-borders.rationale: Its program was a Jewish-majority state with secure borders held behind an iron wall.

revolution-justified.rationale: Revisionists backed armed struggle against the British, including the Irgun, but Jabotinsky favoured a legal parliamentary approach, so adherents split.

central-planning.rationale: Revisionists rejected the socialist planning of the Labor movement and favoured private capital.

socialized-markets.rationale: The worker- or public-owned model was Labor Zionism's, which Revisionists opposed.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Revisionism rejected communism and class struggle and championed bourgeois private capital.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Revisionists backed compulsory arbitration of labor disputes and a ban on strikes during state-building, close to state-set bargaining.

one-party-rule.rationale: Jabotinsky ruled out a police state and Herut was accepted as a parliamentary democratic party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Not an issue; Jabotinsky imagined a state loyal to the British Empire but favoured parliamentary government.

democracy-best.rationale: The mainstream strand favoured British-style liberal democracy and parliamentary methods, despite Jabotinsky's doubts about democracy abroad.

workers-councils.rationale: Council power belongs to the socialist tradition Revisionists opposed.

right-to-secede.rationale: Likud insisted on exclusive Israeli sovereignty between the sea and the Jordan and refused to give up territory.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Irgun carried out armed attacks, and Jabotinsky argued enforced justice is still justice.

war-builds-character.rationale: Betar taught martial discipline and that Jews survive by fighting back, but this is not an explicit doctrine about war's value.

separate-church-state.rationale: Revisionism was neutral on religion; it did not push either strict separation or a religious state.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Jabotinsky stressed that the state need not be Orthodox, and Revisionism did not rest its claims on religious doctrine.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The movement demanded a strong state army and rejected non-state defense of the Jewish national home.

military-superiority.rationale: The iron wall holds that only a force the Arabs cannot overcome secures the Jewish state.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The goal was a state with a Jewish majority, though Arabs would hold full civil rights.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Revisionists explicitly rejected class struggle and put national interests first.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The movement rejected socialist egalitarianism while promising a bourgeois regime would end poverty.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Jabotinsky argued that native populations resist colonists but self-determination should not protect existing possession against landless peoples.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Betar education put the national idea above individual status.

limit-population.rationale: Revisionism sought a large Jewish population and mass immigration, so limiting growth runs against it.

restore-past-order.rationale: The program aimed at building a new state rather than restoring an old order, though it did cite historic right.

direct-action.rationale: The Irgun used direct armed action while the mainstream pursued parliamentary and diplomatic routes.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to a modernising, urban-development program.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: A communist aim that Revisionism rejected.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Revisionists opposed communist distribution and favoured private enterprise.

production-for-use.rationale: Their economics rested on private capital and profit-seeking enterprise.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Revisionists rejected class struggle and Marxist analysis and defended private capital.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Jabotinsky opposed communism and a communist police state.

collective-farming.rationale: Collective kibbutz-type farming was the Labor Zionist model, which Revisionists opposed.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: A Marxist thesis rejected by a movement favouring private capital. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Jabotinsky saw Arabs as a national minority with minority rights, so group status mattered, and the nation took priority over individual status.

organic-representation.rationale: Not part of the program, which favoured parliamentary democracy.

total-state.rationale: Jabotinsky explicitly ruled out a police state of the fascist or communist sort.

national-rebirth.rationale: Revisionism sought a national revival of the Jewish people, state and language.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The aim was a Jewish state on both banks of the Jordan and later all of western Eretz Israel, though framed as historic right rather than imperial expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: A feudal model with no place in a modern parliamentary national movement. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

bound-labor.rationale: Alien to the program. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

universal-morality.rationale: Jabotinsky argued that Zionism is moral and just and that justice enforced is still justice, appealing to a universal standard.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The founding demand: a Jewish-majority state, with Likud calling the right to Eretz Israel eternal and indisputable.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Revisionists planned mass immigration and evacuation of European Jews, and Likud called on diaspora Jews to settle the land.

revive-national-language.rationale: The New Zionist Organization aimed at the revival of the Jewish state and Hebrew language.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Rejected by a movement that stressed class cooperation and private enterprise.

economic-freedom.rationale: Jabotinsky saw private property as necessary for liberty and promoted private initiative.

rule-by-example.rationale: The program relied on law, military force and parliamentary institutions, not rulers' example.

national-self-determination.rationale: The movement's basic principle was Jewish national self-determination in a state, with Jabotinsky saying self-determination means revision.

force-without-un.rationale: Jabotinsky and later Likud relied on force and rejected externally imposed solutions, including UN Resolution 242.

class-collaboration.rationale: Revisionists emphasised national over class interests, rejected class struggle and backed compulsory arbitration.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The movement stressed Jewish tradition and national culture.

dominated-front.rationale: Jabotinsky sought alliance with the British Empire, not a front against the West.

workers-nation.rationale: Revisionists put the national idea ahead of class and rejected international socialism.

ban-interest.rationale: A bourgeois, private-capital program would not ban lending. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Jabotinsky envisioned Arabs with full civil and minority rights, not racial segregation law.

state-class-instrument.rationale: A Marxist thesis rejected by a movement denying class struggle. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

proportional-representation.rationale: The Israeli system was proportional and Revisionist successors operated in it; no stated doctrine though.

national-mission.rationale: Zionism aimed at a Jewish national home rather than exporting a government form.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Herut campaigned as an opposition against the Labor establishment, but the sources do not frame this as corruption.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Revisionists wanted minimal state in industry but a strong state for defense and state-building, and later accepted some social legislation.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Jabotinsky favoured equal civil rights for Arabs in principle, though the Irgun wing opposed power-sharing.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist debate foreign to Revisionism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Jabotinsky described Zionism as colonization yet insisted it is moral and just, so adherents reject the pejorative framing.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Revisionism was neutral on religious questions.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The liberal strand favoured parliamentary democracy, though Jabotinsky argued Arab consent to Zionism would never be voluntary.

population-transfer.rationale: Jabotinsky's statements on transfer were inconsistent, sometimes supportive and sometimes envisioning Arabs in a democracy, and he denied wanting expulsion; Likud pledged not to dispossess anyone.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Betar taught that Jews might strike first, and the Iron Wall defends enforced justice.

vanguard-party.rationale: A Leninist doctrine opposed by Revisionists. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Jabotinsky promised a regime would eliminate poverty but not through priority-to-poor legislation.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Revisionists banned strikes and lockouts during state-building and favoured compulsory arbitration.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Revisionism attributed poverty to the lack of a bourgeois regime rather than population.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Contrary to parliamentary elections favoured by the movement. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

party-controls-media.rationale: Jabotinsky rejected a police state and Herut accepted parliamentary democracy.

party-commands-army.rationale: Revisionists built armed forces for the nation and not as party formations in a state, though Irgun was a party-aligned militia before statehood.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: A radical-egalitarian idea alien to the bourgeois program. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Betar and Hatzohar were disciplined, leader-led organisations; no explicit doctrine.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The movement insisted on sovereignty and rejected externally imposed arrangements.

clerical-rule.rationale: Revisionism was neutral on religion and did not rest its claims on religious authority.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revisionists supported fighting alongside the Allies and cooperated with national armies, and rejected defeatism.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Jabotinsky sought British alliance and the Jewish state loyal to the Empire.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Contrary to the private-property, private-capital program. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

people-in-arms.rationale: Betar and Irgun urged armed Jewish self-defense but the movement also demanded a regular Jewish army.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: After the 1926-27 crises Revisionists shifted toward urban development and private capital against the Labor agrarian ideal.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Revisionists claimed both banks of the Jordan and rejected partition, which resembles reunification of a divided land; the statement is not specifically addressed.

death-penalty.rationale: Likud pledged to eliminate terror organizations and later Likud figures backed executing terrorists; no founding doctrine.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Revisionists treated statehood as the aim and economic transformation as secondary to national independence.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Likud's platform says Judea and Samaria will not be handed to foreign administration and that only Israeli sovereignty will hold between the sea and the Jordan.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The movement favoured private enterprise but never addressed central banking; adherents have no settled line.

collective-defense.rationale: The movement stressed Jewish self-defence behind an iron wall of its own force, yet Jabotinsky also sought alliances with Britain and Poland, so adherents are split.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Likud's platform asserts Israeli sovereignty over Judea and Samaria and rejects the view that held land is occupied or should be given to foreign administration.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Adherents favoured minority rights and later Likud autonomy plans for Arabs, but no settled position on regions keeping their own legal and economic systems.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mainstream Revisionists favoured liberal parliamentary government and civil rights under law.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Revisionism rejected socialism and class struggle in favour of national unity and compulsory arbitration.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: It held that diaspora Jews should emigrate and its platform called for evacuating the diaspora to a Jewish state.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: It replaced Marxist class analysis with a national-spirit view of history.

ban-cartels.rationale: The program stressed private capital but also state arbitration; no settled line on antitrust.

no-bailouts.rationale: No documented position; adherents split between free-enterprise and state-led traditions.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Iron Wall rejects the pretence that colonisation benefits the Arab population, grounding the claim in national self-interest instead.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The movement rejected class-struggle analysis and socialist theory.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The movement stressed national unity and private enterprise without a stated duty of the rich; adherents are split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Revisionism demanded active nation-building, military training and political action, so withdrawal contradicts it.

native-born-offices.rationale: Revisionism backed full civil rights and proportional representation for Arabs as a minority, so offices are not reserved by birth.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Revisionism held that the whole of the Land of Israel on both banks of the Jordan belongs to the Jewish people, and Likud held that no territory will be given up.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Revisionism sought a Jewish majority state with minority rights for Arabs, not leadership by pre-existing inhabitants.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Revisionists backed private enterprise, but Herut and Likud later supported national insurance, so adherents are split.

job-guarantee.rationale: The programme favoured private initiative and compulsory arbitration, not state-guaranteed jobs.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Betar discipline and respect for law coexisted with Irgun rebellion against Mandate law; adherents are split.

informal-organisation.rationale: Betar and the Irgun were disciplined hierarchical organisations built around a national movement and later parties.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The movement rejected socialism and class struggle in favour of private enterprise, so common ownership of productive means is opposed.

cooperative-communities.rationale: It rejected the socialist communal settlement model (kibbutz) in favour of private enterprise and national unity.

majority-settlement.rationale: It demanded mass Jewish colonisation to create a majority, and Likud's platform pledges settlement across the land.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Revisionism founded its demand for a Jewish state on both banks of the Jordan on the Jewish historical bond to the land, ahead of the claims of its Arab residents.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The mainstream favoured liberal parliamentary government and civil rights, including for the Arab minority, rather than suppressing opposition.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The movement never addressed gender identity, and adherents today are split between liberal and conservative views.

assisted-dying.rationale: The sources are silent on assisted dying and adherents are split between liberal and religious-conservative positions.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The iron wall doctrine rests on military strength as the guarantee of the Jewish state, so abolishing armed forces is the opposite of its programme.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The movement never addressed international lenders; a Likud-style stress on national self-reliance is offset by its market orientation, so adherents split.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Revisionist programme and the Likud platform promised equal civil rights to Arab citizens within a Jewish-majority state, so race-based voting was rejected.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Jabotinsky proposed minority civil rights but a Jewish-majority state; executive power-sharing is not clearly stated, so adherents split.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Betar, the Revisionist youth movement, was a uniformed and drilled organisation training youth for national service and defence.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Jabotinsky's Iron Wall initially relied on a foreign (British) force, and the later movement stressed Jewish self-reliance, so the issue is not settled.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Revisionists rejected class struggle and favoured private enterprise and arbitration, but did not address this question directly.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Iron Wall argues that a settlement can only follow a force the other side cannot overcome, which rejects any absolute bar on killing.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Revisionism honoured its fallen fighters, including executed Irgun members, as national heroes and martyrs.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Revisionism demanded a Jewish state with a Jewish majority and mass immigration, against the cultural-centre idea of the Zionist spiritual school.

culture-before-state.rationale: Revisionism was political Zionism that put statehood and military strength first, against cultural Zionism's priority on renewal.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The movement sought a Jewish-majority state but with equal civil rights for Arabs as a minority, so reserving the economy for the majority was not its program.

independent-unions.rationale: The Revisionists opposed the Histadrut and favoured compulsory arbitration of labour disputes, restricting strikes.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The movement rejected socialism and class struggle for national unity, so socialist tests are not its concern.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Private enterprise was favoured but no position on local services is recorded; adherents are split.

municipal-property.rationale: Revisionism backed private enterprise and national unity; communal ownership is contrary to its platform.

person-over-state.rationale: Mainstream Revisionism embraced liberal parliamentary government and civil rights, with Jabotinsky stressing the individual.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Jabotinsky was secular but respected religious tradition in the platform; adherents are split.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The Iron Wall holds force necessary to secure a Jewish state on both banks of the Jordan, which goes beyond pure self-defence.

arms-reduction.rationale: The Iron Wall essay makes military strength the basis of security and of any eventual agreement with the Arabs (s1), so arms reduction runs against it.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The Iron Wall rests on military strength and unflinching force, so refusing orders to fight is contrary to its core.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Revisionists rejected class struggle and favoured compulsory arbitration, so unions bargaining freely was not their model.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The movement stressed private enterprise but the sources name no position on tax credits for low-paid families.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The mainstream favoured liberal parliamentary government and legal means, not overthrowing the state machinery.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Revisionists opposed socialist class-based collective experiments such as the Labour Zionist settlements, preferring private enterprise and national unity.

sacred-nation.rationale: The movement put the nation and national unity above class, though in a liberal rather than mystical register.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Revisionist platform opposed class struggle and favoured compulsory arbitration, putting the nation above class, so a separate workers' party was rejected.

race-social-construct.rationale: Jabotinsky wrote in terms of nation and race, but later adherents are split; the issue was not a doctrinal one.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The movement rejected socialism and class struggle, so defending a planned, nationalised economy is far from its position.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: The Iron Wall holds that the local population will not consent, and the Likud platform vests sovereignty in Israel alone, so a local vote is rejected.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Revisionism rested on the claim that the Jewish people have a historic right to the land on both banks of the Jordan and must defend it, as the Iron Wall essay and Likud platform assert.

close-ties-china.rationale: China was not a factor in the movement's era; later Likud governments have pursued Chinese trade while relying on the United States, so no settled line.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Revisionism was a diaspora-centred movement that sought to protect Jewish communities abroad and press for their rights and evacuation, as the movement's programme and Betar activity show.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Jabotinsky-era program stressed private capital and national unity while later Herut accepted welfare measures, so adherents are split.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Revisionism was a secular national movement that dealt with religion only marginally, and adherents were split between secular and traditionalist outlooks.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Revisionism sought a modern state while honouring Jewish national tradition, but never framed this as a choice; adherents are not clearly in either camp.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Revisionism rejected Marxism and socialist class struggle in favour of private enterprise and national unity, so a labour theory of value is rejected.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Revisionism put nation above class and rejected socialism, but favoured national solidarity including compulsory arbitration between workers and employers; split on this framing.

material-over-identity.rationale: The question is framed for the left, which Revisionism opposed; it put national identity first, and the framing does not map onto it.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Revisionism rejected communism and socialism and favoured private enterprise under parliamentary government, so a communist-led market economy is opposed.

missingStatements.text: The Jewish people should have a state with a Jewish majority on both banks of the Jordan River.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1931 and later Revisionist demand was a Jewish-majority state on both sides of the Jordan, which no existing statement captures.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to the Revisionist territorial programme; covered loosely by territorial-expansion and jewish-state-israel and not a question other ideologies would take sides on.

missingStatements.text: A country should not give up land it claims as its historic homeland in exchange for peace agreements.
missingStatements.rationale: Likud's platform says Judea and Samaria will not be handed to foreign administration and that only Israeli sovereignty will hold between the sea and the Jordan.

missingStatements.text: Peaceful agreement with a local population opposed to settlement is impossible until that population despairs of stopping it by force.
missingStatements.rationale: The Iron Wall argues that no voluntary agreement is possible and that a force the natives cannot overcome must come first.
missingStatements.declined: A specific strategic argument (the Iron Wall) rather than a position other ideologies would take a side on; too narrow for the bank.

notes: The Irgun wing opposed power-sharing with Arabs, while centrist Revisionists favoured liberal democracy. Jabotinsky's statements on transfer were inconsistent. Economics were never fully worked out, so many economic answers are low confidence.
